items.followUp: Define one mole and write the formula for calculating the number of moles from mass and molar mass.

rubric.why: A mole is defined by the number of elementary particles it contains.
rubric.description: Defines one mole using Avogadro's number of particles.
rubric.how: Award for stating that one mole contains about 6.02 × 10²³ entities (atoms, molecules, or ions).

rubric.why: The formula relates the amount of substance to sample mass and molar mass.
rubric.description: Gives the formula for calculating moles.
rubric.how: Award for n = m/M, with n as number of moles, m as mass, and M as molar mass.

modelAnswer: One mole is the amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ elementary particles (Avogadro's number).
Number of moles, n = mass, m ÷ molar mass, M; therefore, n = m/M.

items.followUp: Name the scientists credited with discovering the electron and the neutron.

rubric.why: J. J. Thomson is credited with discovering the electron.
rubric.description: Names the discoverer of the electron.

rubric.why: Goldstein is commonly credited in school texts with discovering the proton through positive (canal) rays; Rutherford later identified the hydrogen nucleus as a proton.
rubric.description: Names the discoverer of the proton.

modelAnswer: The electron was discovered by J. J. Thomson.
The proton was discovered by Eugen Goldstein.

items.followUp: State two limitations of Rutherford's atomic model.

rubric.why: The model could not explain why orbiting electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that orbiting electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, making the atom unstable.

rubric.why: Rutherford's model did not explain the observed line spectra of atoms.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the model could not explain atomic line spectra.

modelAnswer: According to classical theory, revolving electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus; therefore, Rutherford's model could not explain the stability of atoms.
The model could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

items.followUp: Explain why isotopes of an element have different masses but the same atomic number.

rubric.why: Atomic number fixes the number of protons and therefore determines an element's identity.
rubric.description: Explains that atomic number determines the identity of an element.
rubric.how: Award for linking atomic number to proton number and elemental identity.

rubric.why: Atomic mass can vary between isotopes, while the proton number remains unchanged.
rubric.description: Contrasts atomic number with atomic mass.
rubric.how: Award for noting that isotopes have the same atomic number but can have different masses.

modelAnswer: Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom and determines the identity and electronic arrangement of an element.
Atomic mass can vary among isotopes of the same element, but their atomic number remains the same; hence atomic number is the more fundamental property.

items.followUp: Define first ionization energy and state the state of the atom involved.

rubric.why: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom.
rubric.description: Defines ionization energy as energy required to remove an electron.
rubric.how: Award for stating that energy must be supplied to remove an electron.

rubric.why: The standard definition specifies an isolated gaseous atom and formation of a positive ion.
rubric.description: Specifies the gaseous atom and resulting ion.
rubric.how: Award for stating that an electron is removed from an isolated gaseous atom, forming a positive ion.

modelAnswer: Ionization energy is the energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
This removal forms a positive ion.

items.followUp: Which element has the lowest electronegativity, and what is the electronegativity of fluorine relative to other elements?

rubric.why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity among the elements.
rubric.description: Identifies the element with the highest electronegativity.
rubric.how: Award both marks for naming fluorine.

modelAnswer: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of all the elements.

items.followUp: Explain why halogens tend to gain rather than lose an electron.

rubric.why: Halogens have seven valence electrons and need one more to complete their outer shell.
rubric.description: States the halogen valence-shell arrangement and tendency to complete the octet.
rubric.how: Award for stating that halogens have seven outer-shell electrons and need one to complete the shell.

rubric.why: A halogen holds its electrons strongly, so removing one requires substantial energy.
rubric.description: Explains why removal of an electron is difficult.
rubric.how: Award for linking strong attraction for electrons or high ionization energy to the difficulty of removing an electron.

modelAnswer: A halogen atom has seven electrons in its outermost shell and tends to gain one electron to complete its octet.
Its outer electrons are held strongly by the nucleus, so removing an electron requires considerable energy.

items.followUp: State two physical properties of water that are affected by hydrogen bonding.

rubric.why: Extra energy is needed to overcome intermolecular hydrogen bonds, raising boiling and melting points.
rubric.description: Identifies the increased boiling or melting point.
rubric.how: Award for stating that hydrogen bonding raises the boiling point or melting point.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding strengthens attraction between molecules and can increase viscosity and surface tension.
rubric.description: Identifies another physical property increased by hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award for stating that hydrogen bonding increases viscosity or surface tension.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding increases the boiling point and melting point because extra energy is needed to separate the molecules.
It also increases properties such as viscosity and surface tension.
